title: Reading hadith today
hookLine: reading hadith with its context and a teacher

cards: Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. Stop the sentence there and it sounds like a call to back your own side no matter what.

The people who first heard it seem to have stumbled too, because in Sahih al-Bukhari someone asks the Prophet ﷺ: helping him when he's wronged, that we understand, but how do we help him when he's the oppressor?
And the answer turns the whole thing around. By stopping him from oppressing. Half a hadith, heard alone, pointed the opposite way from the whole.

teach.b: First, the whole text. Reports travel now as screenshots and captions, trimmed to fit. A basic habit of hadith study is the one you just heard: find the full report, question and answer, before deciding what it says.
Scholars paid attention to the occasion of a saying, sabab al-wurud: who asked, what had just happened, who was being spoken to.
When Abdullah ibn Amr was told that his body had a right over him, it was because he had been fasting every day and standing in prayer every night.
Lift that line out of its story and it can be made to say almost anything.
Third, the neighbors. A single report sits among others on the same subject, and among the verses of the Qur'an.
Jurists read them side by side, and the schools of law sometimes reached different conclusions from the same texts. That's where this year turns next. Fourth, the person.

teach.h: LOOK AT WHOM YOU LEARN FROM.
teach.b: In the introduction to his Sahih, Imam Muslim records a saying of the early scholar Muhammad ibn Sirin: this knowledge is religion, so look carefully at whom you take your religion from.

The chain didn't stop when the books were finished. Students went on reading the collections aloud in front of teachers, who could say: this word means this, that report explains this one, here the scholars differ.
That's still how this tradition reads hadith at its most careful: the words, the setting, the other texts, and someone who has walked the road before you.

how: Muslims who study hadith read the collections with a teacher, in a class or circle, who explains each report's setting, its other versions, and how scholars have understood it.

o: judging each report by how it sounds to people now
taking a report whole, in its setting, with someone who studied it
reading hadith only in modern translations, without Arabic

games.q: a friend sends you half a hadith that seems to back your side in an argument. what do you do?
o: send it on and win the argument.
find the full report and ask someone who knows it.
decide hadith are too confusing to read at all.
games.why: the first hearers did just that with "help your brother": they asked, and the answer turned the half they'd heard around.

practice: Bring to mind a hadith you've heard quoted, maybe on a screen, and put today's questions to it gently: is that the whole of it, who was being spoken to, what else is said on this? Notice which ones you can't answer.
Then think of one person you could ask, an imam, a teacher, a friend who studies, and hold their face in mind for a breath.

wordCard.voice: Reading hadith today. Taking a report whole, in its setting, beside the other texts, and with someone who has studied it. Today's word.
